candidates.title: An Oregon Parking Lot Was Transformed Into a Forest-Inspired Library
candidates.full_text:
At East County Library in Gresham, Oregon, timber columns rise through gaps in the acoustic ceiling, keeping the structure visually separate from the surfaces around it. Holst Architecture designed this detail to suggest tree trunks reaching toward a canopy. The forest reference is built into the architecture, rather than applied afterward as a decorative theme.

Opened in May 2026, the approximately 95,000-square-foot library serves eastern Multnomah County. Holst led the design, collaborating with Adjaye Associates through the design development phase. Its scale addresses a longstanding imbalance: more than 40 percent of county residents live east of Interstate 205, yet East County previously had the library system’s smallest footprint.

The project replaces an underused parking lot with a public destination connected to transit. A tree-lined pedestrian route links the MAX light rail stop and northern civic space to a terraced entrance plaza on Division Street. That arrangement makes the approach part of the project, giving pedestrians a defined route between transportation and the library’s entrances.

Inside, glulam beams and cross-laminated timber panels form the primary structural system. Double-height entrances and a central living room establish larger clearings within the column grid. Holst paired overhead beams and introduced recessed lines in the timber to give the ceiling depth and rhythm. These choices make the forest analogy legible through construction, without requiring literal representations of branches or leaves.

The building isn’t exclusively timber. Concrete shear walls around the auditorium and along the eastern side provide structural support, with concrete also used around acoustically sensitive spaces. This hybrid approach is worth noting: the material palette responds to different demands rather than treating exposed wood as the answer to every problem.

Holst organizes the plan from active spaces on the west toward focused reading and work areas on the east. Entrances, creative activities, and children’s play occupy the busier edge. Collections and specialized rooms sit toward the center, while window-lined seating provides a quieter destination. The layout acknowledges that a contemporary library needs room for conversation and concentration.

That range includes an audiovisual studio, a creative learning room, indoor and enclosed outdoor children’s spaces, and a rooftop terrace. Two sensory rooms, one oriented toward children and another toward adults, offer adjustable lighting and different ways to engage or withdraw. Community consultation helped shape these provisions, giving the expansive brief specific places to land.

Radiant flooring and rooftop solar panels accompany a LEED Gold target, not a confirmed certification. Beyond those systems, the useful architectural decision is spatial: a large civic building makes room for different levels of participation, including the simple wish to sit quietly with a book.

candidates.title: Razer Raiju V3 Pro Signature Edition wraps a PS5 controller in magnesium and limits it to 1,337 units
candidates.full_text:
Razer’s new flagship PS5 controller is built out of magnesium, and it still weighs just 260 grams. The Raiju V3 Pro Signature Edition wraps the V3 Pro’s tournament kit in an open-air magnesium alloy exoskeleton, then caps production at 1,337 individually serialized units, sold only through Razer’s own store and a short list of RazerStore locations.

The weight deserves a second look. Sony’s DualSense is plastic and weighs 280 grams. This one is metal, it’s full of openings you can see the circuit boards through, and it still comes in 20 grams lighter than the pad it would replace in your hands.

Instead of a solid shell, the Signature Edition runs a polygonal frame with the middle cut away. The boards sit visible under a protective nano coating, the edges are precision-chamfered, and the laser-etched glass touchpad up top carries a semi-transparent tint over the same geometric pattern. It reads more like a display piece than a controller, though every opening is doing structural work.

Metal usually adds grams, so Razer took them back out through the cutouts. Its own lineup gives the cleaner comparison: the standard Raiju V3 Pro, in plastic, weighs 258 grams on Razer’s spec sheet. The magnesium one lands two grams heavier than that and twenty lighter than a DualSense, which is a strange place for a metal controller to end up, and exactly the point of building it this way.

Under the frame it’s the V3 Pro’s working gear. Symmetrical TMR thumbsticks handle aiming, and TMR sensors don’t drift the way potentiometer sticks do, so the dead zones you set stay set. The caps swap in seconds: short convex sticks ride in the controller, tall concave ones sit in the box for players who want the extra leverage on the right stick.

Six extra buttons map however you like. Two claw-grip bumpers sit up top for fingers that never leave the sticks, and four mouse-click back buttons ride underneath, removable when you don’t want them, with blanking covers included. The face buttons are double-shot PBT in tone-on-tone black, the grips are micro-textured TPU, and nothing about the control layout asks you to relearn the standard model.

The symmetrical stick layout keeps the PlayStation arrangement instead of the offset layout most PC pads use, and that suits the double life this controller leads: licensed PS5 pad first, high-polling PC controller second. Whichever machine you’re playing on, the shape under your thumbs stays the one PlayStation players already know.

On PC the controller polls at up to 2,000 Hz over Razer’s HyperSpeed wireless through the included dongle, which is four times the rate most wireless pads report at. It’s officially licensed for PlayStation 5, and Razer rates it for Windows 11 PCs, so one controller covers both machines on a desk.

Tuning runs through the Razer PS Controller App on your phone or Synapse 4 on PC. Stick dead zones, trigger actuation points and button maps all adjust in software, and the controller holds four profiles at once, so a shooter setup and a fighting-game setup ride along without a laptop nearby to swap them.

Each of the 1,337 units carries its own serial number, and the number itself is the old leetspeak gag, chosen on purpose. Razer ships the controller in a vegan leather Signature box with a premium leatherette carrying case, an anodized aluminum torque driver, a USB-A to USB-C cable, the spare stick caps and the back button covers. The Raiju line started in 2016, so this is the tenth-year version of a controller family Razer has been refining for a decade.

If the serialized run isn’t your thing, the regular Raiju V3 Pro Black sells on Amazon right now for $214.99, in stock and shipping. You get the same TMR sticks, the same six remappable buttons and the same 2,000 Hz polling ceiling in a plastic shell that weighs 258 grams. What you give up is the magnesium frame, the glass touchpad and the number stamped into a 1,337-unit run.

So the choice splits cleanly. Players who want the kit buy the standard model today and save whatever Razer ends up asking for the Signature. Collectors and the Raiju faithful buy the metal one for the frame, the serial number and the fact that 1,337 is all there will ever be. Two grams heavier than plastic, twenty lighter than Sony’s pad, and gone once the run sells through.

candidates.title: This fan-made LEGO McDonald’s combo comes with everything except the McFlurry
candidates.full_text:
In 1999, LEGO sold an official McDonald’s restaurant brickset through its Shop at Home catalog in the US, and it was adorably tiny. Set 3438 used 98 pieces to build a little drive-through window, a car, and an umbrella table, with stickers doing most of the branding work. The employee was basically a standard LEGO chef with the logo slapped on his chest. One collector paid $75 for a sealed copy back in 2011, for a set that cost around ten bucks new. Twenty-seven years later, a fan builder thinks the next LEGO McDonald’s should skip the building entirely and go straight for the food.

Called McDonald’s Menu, brickbybrick_’s LEGO Ideas submission rebuilds a classic combo big enough to hold its own on a shelf. There’s a red tray with giant Golden Arches in the middle, a cheeseburger, a red carton overflowing with fries, and a white cup loaded with transparent ice and a striped straw. Zero minifigures, zero drive-through, all lunch. The project went up on October 29 and is already sitting at 1,440 supporters, which tells me a lot of AFOLs (adult fans of LEGO) are hungry. I’m one of them, and I’m writing this before lunch.

Red plates form the tray, finished with a raised, rounded rim and a handle at each end, so it reads as molded plastic instead of a stack of bricks. A big yellow set of Golden Arches sits dead center, breaking up what would otherwise be a whole lot of red. The food is arranged in the classic triangle: burger front left, cup at the back, fries off to the right. It’s the exact layout you’d find on any table at your local McDonald’s around noon. That framing makes the build look like a meal someone just set down, which is half the fun of it.

The cheeseburger starts with a dome of tan curved elements, smooth on top like a plain hamburger bun. Under it sits a red layer that reads as tomato, then bright green leaf pieces fanning out as lettuce, a slice of yellow cheese, and a dark brown patty. Those leaves are a nice bit of NPU (nice part usage, for the uninitiated), taking foliage meant for LEGO gardens and jungles and turning it into a salad. Each layer sticks out at slightly uneven angles, giving the burger that freshly squished look of something just pulled from its wrapper. Real fast food never comes perfectly stacked, and this one looks like it survived a lunch rush.

A pile of yellow plates and bricks spills out of the red fry carton at every angle, some standing tall and some flopped over the edge the way the last few always are. The carton gets the real thing’s shape right, the one McDonald’s introduced in 1970 with a wide mouth for quick scooping and a profile that keeps the fries from falling out. The Golden Arches appear on its face in yellow, the same red-and-yellow combo that has been selling fries for over five decades. Building fries in LEGO is easy, but making them look casually messy takes real effort. My only complaint is that I can’t salt them.

My favorite detail, though, is the drink. The white cup’s top is left open, showing a load of transparent pieces packed in as ice, with a red-and-white striped straw sticking out at a jaunty angle. That straw does three jobs at once. It gives the composition its tallest point, adds a splash of red to an otherwise white element, and nods to a real McDonald’s quirk, since the chain says its straws are slightly wider than average so more Coke hits your taste buds. The ice tells its own story, because McDonald’s pre-chills its syrup and sets the ratio expecting the ice to melt. Leaving the lid off is what lets you see all of it.

Back in 2021, adammark’s McDonald’s Franchise 1955-1969, a walk-up burger stand with a Speedee System kitchen, hit 10,000 supporters and reached the Third 2021 Review. It was one of 36 projects in that round, and Hocus Pocus ended up as the only one approved. brickbybrick_ takes a different route, shrinking the subject from a restaurant down to a single meal sized for a shelf. The build is unlicensed, so those Golden Arches are a fan’s tribute, and any official version would need McDonald’s on board. The two companies have teamed up before, going back to LEGO’s first Happy Meal promotion in 1983, so the precedent exists.

McDonald’s Menu currently has 1,440 supporters and 599 days left to reach its next milestone of 5,000. LEGO Ideas runs on community momentum: fans submit their builds, supporters rally behind the ones they love, and projects that hit 10,000 get reviewed by LEGO for a shot at becoming real sets.
